hits.full_text: A CLUB JUST ASKED MY FLY TO DJ THEIR ENTIRE NIGHT Yesterday I got a message from a club called Neon Hive with a completely insane proposal: they wanted my FLY to run their next party from start to finish and choose everything by itself. They wanted no human controlling the set. So I gave them my code, connected the system to their DJ setup and let the fly take over the booth for the night. From that moment, every decision was hers. Fly picked what played next, controlled the decks and kept the party moving while hundreds of people danced, sang and had absolutely no idea who was actually running the music. The weirdest part is watching the footage afterward. You see a packed nightclub going completely crazy while this tiny fly is sitting behind the decks with its headphones on, casually running the entire night like this is what it was born to do. Nobody in the crowd knows their DJ is an insect. And somehow, the party just keeps going. Neon Hive might have been the first club brave enough to hire a FLY

A CLUB JUST ASKED MY FLY TO DJ THEIR ENTIRE NIGHT

Yesterday I got a message from a club called Neon Hive with a completely insane proposal: they wanted my FLY to run their next party from start to finish and choose everything by itself. They wanted no human controlling the set.

So I gave them my code, connected the system to their DJ setup and let the fly take over the booth for the night. From that moment, every decision was hers.

Fly picked what played next, controlled the decks and kept the party moving while hundreds of people danced, sang and had absolutely no idea who was actually running the music.

The weirdest part is watching the footage afterward. You see a packed nightclub going completely crazy while this tiny fly is sitting behind the decks with its headphones on, casually running the entire night like this is what it was born to do.

Nobody in the crowd knows their DJ is an insect. And somehow, the party just keeps going.

Neon Hive might have been the first club brave enough to hire a FLY.

Different angle, same bruise: you did not lose because the model was weak. You lost because the loop never met a stranger who cared. Ten thousand dollars bought tooling, tokens, and optimism. It did not buy distribution.

hits.full_text: I TURNED A FLY INTO A WELDER AND GAVE IT ITS OWN FABRICATION LAB I don't know why this seemed like a reasonable experiment, but now there is a robotic fly standing inside a fabrication workshop operating a live welding arc. The machine moves around the metal surface while a bright arc cuts across it, drawing a pattern one movement at a time. The fly is right there in the middle of the process, moving its mechanical legs and wings while its camera eyes watch the work from inches away. And the setup is way more serious than it has any right to be. The system is running around 85 amps and 12.2 volts, with the thermal array pushing past 1,400 degrees while the wire extension keeps advancing across the surface. Then you look at the other half of the screen. 166,700 retained neurons. 25.5 million approximate synapses. 15,378 neurons fired. The entire connectome is being visualized beside the fabrication process, with neural activity lighting up the brain while the robotic fly is working. So technically this isn't just a fly holding a welding tool. It's a tiny nervous system connected to a machine that can actually build things. I think I just gave a fly its first job in heavy industry

I TURNED A FLY INTO A WELDER AND GAVE IT ITS OWN FABRICATION LAB

I don't know why this seemed like a reasonable experiment, but now there is a robotic fly standing inside a fabrication workshop operating a live welding arc.

The machine moves around the metal surface while a bright arc cuts across it, drawing a pattern one movement at a time. The fly is right there in the middle of the process, moving its mechanical legs and wings while its camera eyes watch the work from inches away.

And the setup is way more serious than it has any right to be. The system is running around 85 amps and 12.2 volts, with the thermal array pushing past 1,400 degrees while the wire extension keeps advancing across the surface.

Then you look at the other half of the screen. 166,700 retained neurons. 25.5 million approximate synapses. 15,378 neurons fired. The entire connectome is being visualized beside the fabrication process, with neural activity lighting up the brain while the robotic fly is working.

So technically this isn't just a fly holding a welding tool. It's a tiny nervous system connected to a machine that can actually build things.

I think I just gave a fly its first job in heavy industry.

hits.full_text: this is f*cking gold Uber engineers built their own AI coding assistant for six months, then killed it on purpose. 100 million lines across six monorepos. zero new headcount approved. so they pointed agents at the debt instead. every workflow gets modelled as a state machine. deterministic steps call a tool: prepare the mocks, run the build, index the repo. only the steps that need judgement call a model. red CI feeds the error back to the model the same way it would to a person, and it loops until green. the Java to Kotlin migration is where it bites. 10 million lines. on the current trend it finishes in 8 years. so they mined their own history: replay thousands of past migrations, run today's tooling over the same commits, diff it against what the developer actually shipped. that delta is everything the tooling was missing. then the constraint that makes the whole thing safe. the model is never allowed to write the migrated code. it writes the AST rule. the rule is deterministic, gets reviewed once, and converts the repo forever. 8 years becomes 18 months. same cycle on tests. generate, build, fix its own failures, validate the asserts against the comment on the function, refactor into the house pattern. 29 manual steps, one loop, runs to 80% coverage. the leverage was never the model. it was the veto.

hits.full_text: I GAVE KIMI K3 THREE HUNDRED AGENTS AND ONE NIGHT. ZERO WAKE-UPS. four tools. five hooks. budget forty five minutes, finished in forty one. the hooks did the work I used to do by hand: 1,689 tool calls checked before they touched anything 1,689 answers checked on return 21 failures retried with the reason attached 1 draft held in a queue for me 1 run written into the record morning: one file to read, two decisions. seven disciplines everyone named separately are parts of one machine. the prompt is a file. the context is an assembler. the tools are typed. the loop is a runner that stops on counts. the memory is a graph. the check is a verifier the agent does not control. the frame around all of it is the harness. K3 leads the frontend arena right now. 1,679 against 1,631 and 1,618. first in six of seven domains. seventeen places up in one update. which is why it sits behind one line and nothing else in the system knows its name. the swap test: change that line, run the night again. passed. format held, the run still ended on counts, last week's corrections still loaded, nothing wrote outside its folder. whatever breaks after a swap was never the model. it was your harness hiding inside a prompt. save this.

why this matters: AI access is becoming the new digital divide, millions of people are just discovering AI right now and can't justify $20-200/mo subscriptions. we give them the best free routes: clean, current, verified

what's coming:
1) direct API key giveaways integrated into the site
2) VC conversations forming (real numbers back the pitch now)
3) marketing push funded entirely by creator fees I've earned

$HOP now lives on its own, I don't hold it, but the creator fees mean I can build freeLLM for a long time without external pressure

> 100K site visits coming this month

a note on today's launch: we tried launching a second token to boost trust in the ecosystem. our team genuinely loved the scientists' discovery and wanted to back it. it didn't take off, but we're still ready to send the collected fees to the researcher as promised

that part matters more to us than the market reaction

I'm not going anywhere, this is only the beginning
